The Periodic Table of Chemical Elements holds a unique place among scientific accomplishments. It is a simple-looking and easily accessible reference tool as well as a research tool. It is also significant in almost every scientific discipline; researchers from all sciences continue to mine the relationships the table organizes.
This lighthouse/beacon of order amid the chaos of the physical world has inspired an animation that has produced remarkable on-line versions, all easily accessible to everyone — even set to music.
And because 2019 marks the 150th anniversary of the discovery of the relationships that underlie the Periodic Table by Russian Dmitri Mendeleev and the centennial of the founding of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), the organization that oversees scientific nomenclature and, de facto, is the keeper of the Periodic Table, ensuring it is both up-to-date and accurate, the United Nations has declared 2019 the International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements (IYPT 2019), to celebrate one of the most familiar and powerful scientific accomplishments in human history.
The International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements will begin with a formal launch of the Year at UNESCO offices in Paris, with presentations on the past, present and future of the system, capped with a lecture by Dutch chemist Ben Feringa, recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
In February, there will be a two-day symposium on the contributions of female researchers to the contemporary Periodic Table, organized by UNESCO with IUPAC, the International Union of the History and Philosophy of Science, the European Chemical Society, Real Sociedad Española de Química and the University of Murcia. There will also be a Global Women’s Breakfast, a single-day event on February 12 run by local organizers, including Canadian events taking place across the country.
In July, the World Chemistry Congress and the IUPAC General Assembly will complete the Periodic Table of Younger Chemists, with room to add Canadian nominations, such as Kelly Summers from the University of Saskatchewan for copper and Ernest Awoonor-Williams of Memorial University for zinc.
The British educational organization 1001 Inventions is mounting a multimedia initiative that will cover the inquiry spanning more than 1200 years that culminated in today’s well-organized Periodic Table.
The 102nd Canadian Chemistry Conference and Exhibition (CCCE 2019) will celebrate the elements and the variety of Canadian chemistry, with conference abstracts grouped according to the most prominently featured element. The Chemical Institute of Canada is a big fan of the table and is offering members a chance at their own copy of a remarkable physical representation of it, the ElemenTree, developed by the late Fernando Dufour, a professor at Collège Ahuntsic in Montreal. The CIC has offered a number of these keepsakes, and look for the chance to obtain one, and other IYPT 2019 announcements, in 2019.

Like many communities in the Canadian Shield, Haliburton is known for its wild highlands and countless lakes. The forestry economy that used to sustain the region has been replaced by reliance on tourism. Locals are quick to chide the seasonal urbanites, yet the capital that comes in from the city is necessary to keep the region economically stable. This story plays out across much of Ontario and other regions of North America. While the prosperity seems to be waning, the communities that are the least self-reliant feel the pressure the most. Importing most of our products means that our capital must come from outside the region. Tourism brings in a lot of cash, but it ties our fortunes to one industry, much like the towns that were abandoned after one big employer left. This only works if tourists exist. With more and more communities turning to tourism, the competition for market share heats up. If the status quo continues, this is not a concern, as the global economy will recover and tourism dollars will continue to prop up the community. What if urban disposable income were to collapse, and the tourists stayed home? Many locals want to be prepared for such a change. It’s a common movement in small towns across the continent.
Cheap food, goods, and energy come from far-away jurisdictions, far from most small communities. Even in Southern Ontario, with its rich farmland, we are growing mostly corn and soybeans to feed our livestock. We import a considerable amount of food and manufacturing has been gutted long ago. Our energy rests on tenuous international relationships and unwieldy infrastructure. Community groups have formed to fill the void should the system fail.
Haliburton has been putting a focus on food and agriculture. If our food system were to be disrupted, we will be lucky if we have any food at all. Even now, our food system does not reach everyone who needs it. Rural poverty is glaring and access to healthy food is inadequate. Reforming the food system can help us prepare for change, and address the uneven distribution of good food.
It’s a tragedy that we had some self-reliance in food, energy, and manufactured goods in the past. Our skills were broad and well-honed. Good land was in production, and we had the infrastructure to grow and process food right here at home. Gaps were filled with inter-regional supply lines connecting neighbouring communities. In only a couple generations, globalization has eroded small-community self-reliance. We now rely on cheap labour in other jurisdictions, and cheap energy to deliver goods. We’ve relied on corporate imperialism, and polluting energy that will eventually doom us. And for what? So we can have affordable food and goods? We’ve traded self-determination for convenience. Even with cheap food, many families can’t feed themselves well. (Food is a scapegoat, the real drain on our resources are the predatory practices of banks, utilities, insurers, governments, and everyone else after your wallet.)
Vulnerabilities are now clear. More and more people are joining the food system reform movement. The first challenge we must face is the repeated insistence that we can’t grow food on the Canadian Shield. We will not be the capital of corn and soybeans, or expansive feed lots. But we can accumulate small-scale enterprises that can reach critical mass to feed our community. Our soil will not withstand the rape of cash crops, our land is unsuitable for mechanization, we can’t repeat past failures. There are agricultural systems that grow soil over time, crops that thrive in this climate. There’s hope and innovation. There is a history of farming in Haliburton.
The next step after finding our mettle is to collaborate. Reforming the food system is not a step one through twelve. It must happen concurrently, with every puzzle piece in place at once. A storeowner can’t promote local produce without a supply. A farmer can’t grow without a market. A bakery can’t mill flour from uncleaned grain. A restaurant can’t sell meat that hasn’t been processed in an appropriate facility. Despite the supportive organizations, it is the individual entrepreneurs and families that are taking the risk to build the new food system. We all must co-ordinate and share the risk. Haliburton is standing on the edge. Not having faith in the status quo is not enough. Watching from the comfort zone is not an option. What is needed is a collective willingness to step forward despite the risks.

Most scopes have their windage and elevation adjustments referenced to MOA (minute of angle). Each click is usually 1/4 MOA (some scopes are 1/8 MOA). Instead of using the true value of MOA, which is a fraction of an inch at 100 yards, shooters will refer to it as a fraction of an inch because that number is easy to visualize and doesn’t require the use of a calculator. This number is close enough for practical purposes, especially up to a few hundred yards. The real difference is only 0.47 inch at 1000 yards.
For serious target shooting and increasing distances, the value of MOA versus sight adjustment becomes more essential to know.
To understand MOA, you first have to understand arc angles. An arc angle is measured in degrees. There are 360 degrees in a full circle and each degree is composed of 60 minutes of arc. The distance covered by an arc angle is relative to the circumference (total distance around the circle). Once you know the radius of a circle, you can easily find the circumference by using pi (π). Pi is the ratio of the circumference to the diameter (radius x 2) and is a constant regardless of the size of the circle. The precise value of pi is unknown to man, but is normally resolved to 3.1416 or 3.141.
For instance, a circle with a 6 inch radius would have a circumference of (6 x 2) x 3.1416 = 12 x 3.1416 = 37.6992 inches. So, 1 degree would equal 37.6992 / 360 = 0.1047 inch at 6 inches from the center of the circle. And 1 minute would equal 0.1047 / 60 = 0.001745 inch at 6 inches from the center of the circle. Knowing the MOA value allows you to calculate its value at any distance. 6 inches is 1/600th of 100 yards (100 yards x 36 inches) / 6 inches = 600. So MOA at 100 yards equals 1.047 inches (0.001745 x 600). Scaling, 50 yards is 1/2 the 100 yard value; 70% at 70 yards; twice at 200 yards; 6 times at 600 yards; and so on. The difference between thinking in inches versus MOA is 0.47 inch at 1000 yards. Four clicks would equal a 1.047 inch change at 100 yards for scopes with 1/4 MOA per click. Group size in inches: You should spell out ‘inch’ as the symbol (") is inaccurate and misleading since it also means ‘second of angle’ (1/60 of a minute of angle). You should write ‘1 inch’ not 1".
You could write 1' (the symbol for minute of angle) but it may mislead those who are thinking in feet.
Using MOA allows you to easily calculate the value to any distance, from the center of the circle or the muzzle of the barrel. MOA is part of our only universal language, mathematics. Rifle precision in inches is also scalable to other distances, but you need both distance and inch measure (e.g. 1 inch @ 100 yards). With an angle, only the angle measure is needed. For example, 0.73 inch @ 100 yards versus 0.7 MOA (0.73 / 1.0472 = 0.697). Practically equal (1 MOA = 1.047 inch @ 100 yards) but the MOA expression is more concise and no distance is included. Two sites to continue the discussion on MOA: What Is MOA and Is It Really an Inch At 100 Yards? and Mil-dots and Minutes-of-angle, From a Technical Perspective.
Metric countries often use 27.77 mm @ 100 meter. This is the same proportion as 1 MOA = 1.000 inch @ 100 yard.
When shooting at long ranges with varying distances, it is wise to know the actual value of each adjustment, especially if you have changed the settings in the field. Not all scopes are precisely calibrated to MOA or the inch. One method is to shoot from a solid bench rest and find the center of the group using the Average Group Radius method. Without reaching your scope adjustment limit, make and record as many elevation clicks as you need to keep the group on the target, at the same aiming point. Now, find the center of the second group using the Average Group Radius method. Return the elevation to the previous setting. Measure the distance between the two group centers and divide by the number of elevation clicks used for group two. That is the calculated value of each click at that distance. For high power rifles, the target should be no less than 100 yards as some projectiles may not stabilize at shorter distances and give a false indication of their true performance.

Our planet has been thoroughly explored from its core to the surface, and it seems that we are ready to embark on space travel. But this amazing world is still surprising us with many things. Today we would like to share with you 13 unsolved mysteries about our planet.
13. We have never reached the mantle
Seismologists say that the inner core of the Earth is solid, and the outer core is liquid and molten. Then comes the mantle, which floats on the crust. The composition of the mantle is unknown as it has never been reached. The depth of the mantle varies from 30 km to 2,900 km. The deepest well we have managed to drill is the Kola borehole in Russia, and it has only reached a depth of 12.3 km.
12. Poles can change
The magnetic poles can move, and even change their direction, and it has happened many times before. The latest switch took place 10 million years ago, and it is likely to recur. However, no one knows why it happens.
11. The Earth had two moons
According to astronomers, our planet had two satellites about 4.6 million years ago. The second one was approximately 1,200 km in diameter and it had the same orbit as the Moon. But they collided with each other. This cataclysm may explain why the Moon has two different sides.
10. Earthquakes occur on the Moon
Surprisingly, not many people know that earthquakes also happen on the Moon. But they are much weaker than the terrestrial ones, and they are very rare. A theory says that these phenomena are caused by the tidal forces of the Sun and Earth, as well as by falling meteorites.
9. Earth spins fast
Our planet rotates at a speed of 1,600 km/h, and it moves around the Sun at a speed of 108,000 km/h. But we feel the movement only when the speed changes. If the speed is constant, and there is gravity, we do not feel the movement.
8. Time is growing
620 million years ago, a day on Earth lasted only 21.9 hours. It seems that the Earth is slowing down, and it slows down by about 70 msec per 100 years. It will take 100 million years for a day to last 24 hours.
7. Earth’s gravity is strange
The Earth is not a perfect sphere, so there are areas where gravity is strong, and where it is weak. For example, the Hudson Bay in Canada has a weak gravity, because the lower density is caused by the glaciers that rapidly melted.
6. Hottest and coldest places
The hottest place on Earth is Aziziya, Libya, where the temperature reaches +58°С. The coldest place is the Antarctic, where it can be as cold as -73°С. The lowest temperature that has been observed is at the Russian Vostok Station, where it was -89.2°С on July 21, 1983.
5. Severe pollution
This is not really news. But astronauts say that when they saw the Earth from space in 1978, it was different. The space debris and waste are turning the blue, green, and white planet into a brown, gray, and black one.
4. Composition: iron, oxygen, silicon
The composition of the Earth is as follows: 32.1% iron, 30.1% oxygen, 15.1% silicon, 13.9% magnesium. About 90% of the iron is thought to be located in the core of the Earth. Most of the oxygen is in the Earth’s crust, which contains 47%.
3. Purple Earth
It is believed that the ancient plants did not use chlorophyll, but retinal to absorb light. This reflected red and blue light, but not green, which gave the Earth a purple color. Some bacteria still use retinal.
2. Hidden ocean
Beneath the surface of the Earth, there is a huge water pool located at a depth of 410-660 km. It is 2.7 billion years old, and it was found with the help of ringwoodite in the mantle. The water is under immense pressure, and the volume of it is enough to fill the Earth’s oceans three times. There is a theory that the oceans appeared on Earth as a result of an explosion of an underground ocean.
1. Life on Mars
After years of speculation, there are now encouraging signs that a vital molecule for life is on Mars. It was seen in formations in the Gale crater. There are also large carbon-based molecules that remain in the Martian soil, and it is not just contamination from the rover. This suggests that Mars had life long before Earth.

Avalanche vs Zener Breakdown in Diodes
In a basic semiconductor, a junction is formed due to the interaction of the p-type and n-type of material. The junction can be heavily or lightly doped based on the circumstances. A basic p-n diode conducts in a forward bias. In a reverse bias, it can’t conduct but breakdowns arise. This is because of the carrier multiplication and the high concentration of doping at the junction.
There are two types of breakdowns that occur in a reverse bias. They are:
• Avalanche breakdown
• Zener breakdown
What is Avalanche Breakdown?
Under reverse bias, a diode is non-conducting. However, there is some movement of the carriers due to minority carriers. The reverse current is due to the movement of minority charge and is known as reverse saturation current. This reverse saturation current is responsible for the avalanche breakdown. The junction is the interface of the p and n type of material. The depletion region is present in this junction. Both types of carriers are present in the junction in majority and minority carriers. In a reverse bias, the focus is on the minority carriers i.e. the electrons in the p-type material and the holes in the n-type material. The depletion width of the region is variable and depends on the bias supplied. In a reverse bias, the region becomes wider and it affects the working of the diode. However, the minority carriers gain enough kinetic velocity to overcome the junction barrier. Collisions occur and hence free charges are generated. The process continues and the number of free carriers increase due to carrier multiplication. This leads to the reverse current flow, avalanche breakdown. This can damage the junction completely and the process is non-refundable (irreversible).
What is Zener Breakdown?
When the p and n type of material interact, a junction is formed and a depletion region exists at the junction. The width of this region also depends on the doping concentration i.e. light or heavy. The width of this region is inversely related to the doping concentration i.e. heavy doping leads to a minimum width and vice versa. A highly doped junction undergoes the zener breakdown. A minimum width of the depletion region means that there are free charges present which tend to cross the junction. Hence, the highest intensity of the electric field leads to rapid carrier movement which in turn gives the free carriers and the reverse current. This eliminates the depletion region and hence zener breakdown. The depletion region returns once the reverse voltage is removed. In this way, breakdown types under reverse bias are discussed.
Avalanche and Zener Diodes
Avalanche diode: This diode is designed to operate in reverse bias and the junction is lightly doped. This diode falls in a special category and is represented with the same symbol for zener and avalanche diodes.
A basic p-n diode can’t operate in reverse bias and a special diode is required, which is normal in forward bias and tolerates the reverse currents. This is the zener diode with a good doping concentration at the junction.
Difference between Zener and Avalanche Breakdown
Both breakdowns occur in the reverse bias. Zener breakdown has a comparatively lower voltage than avalanche breakdown. The avalanche breakdown is because of collisions between the carriers and the Zener breakdown is because of high electric field intensity. The depletion region in an avalanche breakdown is thick and in the Zener breakdown is thin. The doping at the junction in an avalanche breakdown is minimum and in the Zener breakdown is high. In an avalanche breakdown, a pair of electrons and holes are produced and in the Zener breakdown are mainly electrons. The electric field in an avalanche breakdown is low and in the Zener breakdown is strong. The temperature coefficient in an avalanche breakdown is positive and in the Zener breakdown is negative. The ionization in an avalanche breakdown is due to the collision effect and in the Zener breakdown is due to the strong field. The breakdown voltage and temperature in an avalanche breakdown are directly related and in the Zener breakdown are inversely. After breakdown, the voltage in an avalanche breakdown tends to vary whereas the voltage in the Zener breakdown is unaffected. The junction in the avalanche breakdown is destroyed completely and can’t be recovered whereas the junction in the Zener breakdown returns to the normal state once the reverse voltage is removed.

Hidden costs are what kill.
You spend time hunting for the best and cheapest cellphone, but when you finally buy it, the system-access fee comes as a shock. The education system is the same. You invest to make the best and cheapest system, but once you get in, the student-activity fees come as a surprise.
The cost of learning outside the classroom is staggering. Some students pay massive fees to participate in sports, drama, art or clubs. The act of being involved in your school’s life costs money, and excelling at a sport has a financial penalty. The Ontario education system has an ingrained barrier to experiential learning, which is a systematic barrier that directly challenges poverty reduction and equity in education. It is something the Ministry of Education must confront.
The Ministry of Education is asking school boards for a “snapshot” of the fees that are charged to students. Tomorrow, the Toronto District School Board will debate a motion to create a standard board-wide fee, the first step in gaining control over these charges.
But why do extracurriculars matter? The Ministry of Education definitions treat extracurriculars as an “extra,” something over and above the basic education. But extracurriculars are crucial to building a school community, letting students own their education, to work of their own volition and to achieve their own goals.
Experiential learning can be the difference between an engaged and a disengaged student. Children are fighting obesity and sometimes the best way to teach character education is on a football field. We need more access, not less. The Ministry of Education must open the doors for engaged, healthy, well-behaved students.
School boards need to understand the hidden costs of extracurriculars. More than 77 per cent of schools charge some form of activity fee, and prices are up more than 50 per cent. Most high schools charge an activity card at the start of the term, averaging $35. This is the start of a long litany of costs. In a study of a provincial-barometer board, the cost of one team membership could be as high as $455. There is no way to “buy in bulk.” The cost of joining volleyball plus rugby can be near $1,000. If you add on student council or drama, the cost is like university tuition.
The high costs are a problem, but the message being sent is detrimental. When you win a tournament, you have to pay for the next one. Students are penalized for doing well. That can discourage excellence in extracurriculars.
The fact that school boards are often unaware of fees is scary. Schools charge fees on a club-by-club basis, without any central authority to oversee the amounts. In a study of the average board, the fees charged had a massive range, even between schools a few blocks apart. The conclusion? Boards have no handle on the fees students are asked to pay to explore their talents outside the classroom.
Fees are a major challenge to equity. Some schools are more affordable than others. And some sports are cheaper at one school than another. Lower-income students are faced with fees that limit their participation, worsening the trials of fitting in and succeeding. If we are going to build a truly equitable system, a key component to poverty reduction, we need to remove the fees.
Here are the first steps: First, each board should find out how much students are asked to pay. Then the Ministry of Education can begin funding extracurriculars through non-profit organizations and other ministries, and phase out fees. Remove the barrier to this invaluable part of a school experience. Reach every student in Ontario with a quality education, including the invaluable experience of experiential learning.

I’m studying up on some boring facts for my exam tomorrow, but I just can’t concentrate. I give up and decide to watch a documentary on a fascinating subject instead. The next day, I can’t remember a single fact from my studying, but I remember every tiny detail from the documentary.
It’s easier to learn interesting material than boring facts, but exactly how curiosity affects memory is still a mystery. There’s also comparatively little known about how memories are formed and stored in the brain.
The first major insight into human memory came with the case of Henry Gustav Molaison (H.M.), one of the most studied patients in the history of neuroscience. H.M. suffered from epilepsy and had surgery at the age of 27 to remove brain areas thought to be responsible for his seizures. Although the surgery worked for his epilepsy, it caused a severe case of anterograde amnesia, an inability to form new memories, and he spent the next 50 years of his life in a steady present. This inability to form new memories was attributed to the removal of the medial temporal lobes. Later experiments showed that a structure within this region, the hippocampus, plays a key role in learning and memory.
Decades of research into the mechanisms of memory have identified one potential mechanism: long term potentiation (LTP). LTP occurs when two neurons are stimulated together multiple times. With each stimulation, the electrical connection between them becomes stronger, allowing for better signal transmission between the two. These strengthened connections are thought to underlie the formation of new associations and storage of new memories.
How do complex psychological concepts like curiosity fit into this picture? A recent study in the journal Neuron examined the effect that curiosity has on learning. Study subjects were shown a series of trivia questions, and were asked to rate their curiosity about each question’s answer. During the study, brain activity was monitored in an MRI scanner while subjects were shown a selected question, and then its answer. Before the answer was shown, the subjects were also shown a picture of a neutral face, unrelated to the trivia question task. After the MRI scan, subjects were tested on their memory for both the trivia answers and the faces.
The researchers found that subjects’ memory for the trivia questions and faces was improved by curiosity. The curiosity ratings were also associated with higher activation of the nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra, and ventral tegmental area, brain areas that had previously been linked to extrinsic reward-related memory (memory of rewards coming from outside the world, like food or money). However, the reward here was the curiosity being satisfied, coming from within. This suggests the existence of a common mechanism shared between extrinsic and intrinsic reward-related memory. The authors suggest that this mechanism may involve the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter that has already been linked to learning and extrinsic reward.
Can we harness curiosity to help us learn? Possibly. It’s possible that drugs that act on the dopaminergic system could one day boost learning and memory, acting on the same circuits as learning from interesting material. For now, however, the message for educators is that they can tap into a student’s intrinsic reward system by keeping lessons interesting.

3D printing is a technology that was developed in the 1980s and has since become a staple in many medical uses. It helps surgeons in a number of ways, including providing them with patient-specific organ replicas to practise on before performing complicated operations, and providing them with surgical tools and custom-made prosthetics.
This technology has the potential to help alleviate some of the limits of organ transplantation, by providing personalised tissue engineering scaffolds, in situ tissue defect repair with cells, and even directly printing implants.
Researchers at the University of Birmingham in the UK have developed biodegradable polymer inks to take this technology a step further.
The resin inks, developed by Andrew Dove, founder of 4D Medicine, are based on aliphatic polycarbonates. Unlike other polycarbonates, these do not contain any aromatic groups between the carbonate linkages, and so are less rigid. Dove uses thiol-ene click chemistry to crosslink cyclic carbonate monomers, thereby creating 3D polycarbonate structures that can be printed flexibly.
“A big step was in the precise design of the monomer and the monomer mixture,” he explains. “We have multiple carbonate monomers so we can make resins with different cured mechanical properties, such as being able to be tuned to a specific degradation rate.”
“The ability to tune properties is a big advantage of this chemistry – we can control the microstructure, the macroscopic shape, everything – it’s quite unusual,” Dove adds.
The potential range of applications for the technology is wide, and the company’s first aim is to develop devices that can be used to fill tissue voids after intrusive surgery, for example, after breast cancer removal surgery, where the recovery is a big problem and tissue can be difficult to reconstruct, requiring multiple operations.
“We can print the devices into a unique support structure for the tissue to regrow in after the tumour has been removed,” Dove explains. “Scaffolds can be used to fill the tumour void and help direct radiotherapy, which can improve outcomes and survival rates. After the scaffolds degrade, only natural tissue remains.”
“The devices can be any shape or size and our data show there is no real reaction when they are implanted,” Dove adds. “The thiol-ene chemistry also avoids potentially toxic residual acrylate groups that other biomaterial scaffolds rely on. We have completed a four month rat study, and we are currently doing further animal studies where we implant for shorter and longer periods of time, to see how the device performs across the lifecycle. We are also looking at paediatric uses, such as musculoskeletal problems, where bespoke printed products in different sizes can fit the growing child’s body.”
“We are designing the devices, studying their performance, looking at what patients want,” Dove concludes.
Dove and his business partner, Andrew Weems, spun out 4D Medicine from the University of Birmingham to move the technology towards market approval. Weems was instrumental in the development of the technology and, as a PhD student, contacted Dove to discuss the possibility of linking their 3D printing and shape memory experience together, and how this could be used in biomedical applications.
Weems was subsequently awarded a Whitaker International Program fellowship to work with Dove, and quickly made fast progress, giving him the opportunity to do something impactful.
Weems later secured Innovate UK Innovation and Commercialisation of University Research (Icure) funding, financing the researchers to explore the commercial potential of the technology.
Both funding rounds were essential, according to Dove, who explains that funding is always the biggest hurdle. “The Whitaker fellowship was a turning point because it was difficult to get funding for such an idea,” he adds.
Dove and Weems won the Royal Society of Chemistry Emerging Technologies competition in 2018.
The pair are currently looking to secure investment to complete the final steps to toxicology data proving the safety of the devices to regulators. “The regulatory hurdles for medical devices are big, and there is still much work to do in terms of proving the material safety and going through all the steps to approval,” Dove explains. “However, our target application, plus our material, should mitigate the risk. The initial results we are seeing point us in the right way, and it is looking really good.”

This year, Penn Vet New Bolton Center (NBC) dairy health experts are seeing a higher number of pneumonia cases in dairy cows. These cases are primarily among growing heifers and calves, due to wide temperature swings and wet-warm weather in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
NBC offers the following tips to area producers on how to prevent and manage pneumonia in their dairy cows:
Ventilation is key to proper air quality and cooling capacity required to prevent illness. Keep curtains and windows open to allow for air flow. For older farms, consider installing a forced or tube installation system in barns. All operations benefit from an air-quality and air-flow test.
Vaccination is a key part of preventing pneumonia, as long as it is used correctly. Consult your veterinarian to develop an operation-specific plan or have them come out to make recommendations. Consider adding pneumonia-specific vaccines just before the hardest times of the year, such as early and late winter. Some intranasal vaccines have proven to be especially helpful, as they provide better localized immunity in the airways.
Minimizing stress is important, especially in the winter months. Avoid or minimize additional stressors to animals such as transporting animals, excessive intermingling, and bringing in new stock from outside sources or sale barns if at all possible.
Monitor animals regularly for signs of illness and take temperatures of any that are showing symptoms. Early recognition of illness gives the best chance for effective treatment and prevents long-term damage.
If an outbreak of pneumonia does occur, fast and aggressive treatment is key. Treat affected animals early and consider isolating them to limit the spread of infection. Blanket treatments, including feed-through antibiotics, can work for larger outbreaks. Consult your veterinarian first.

This COVID-19 pandemic is hard to live through, a generational crisis that has struck us like a night-time thief and upended our lives. Our governments are grappling with how to revive the economy and reshape what is acceptable in terms of social interactions, but another battle is being fought by each of us, individually, alone.
We forget that our mental health has also been ravaged and undernourished, starving for relief. Our stress meters have been long in the red, and the prognosis is bleak for certain demographics.
Everyone responds to stress in different ways. Some can handle earth-shaking changes and others fret over minutiae. Regardless of tolerance, the pandemic has been especially bad for the following groups of people, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention:
- People at higher risk for severe illness (older people and anyone of any age with underlying conditions).
- Children and teens.
- People who are caring for family members or loved ones.
- Health care providers and first responders.
- Essential workers in the food industry.
- People with existing mental health conditions.
- Substance users or those with substance use disorder.
- People who have lost jobs, experienced reduced hours or other major changes in employment.
- People with disabilities or developmental delay.
- People who are socially isolated (living alone, in rural or frontier areas).
- Some racial and ethnic minority groups.
- People who don’t have access to information in their primary language.
- People who are experiencing homelessness.
- People living in congregate (group) settings.
The first of five tips to keep your stress in check: Imagine yourself 200,000 years ago, resting by a watering hole after a hunt, with laughter. Then you hear a rustle in the bush, and there’s a tiger in the dark. Your heart pounds, and beads of sweat form. That’s because when you’re in danger, your heart quickens and your breathing quickens, and your muscles tense up — all of this is to provide heightened alertness and brain activity. It’s a design by nature to put the body in gear for precarious situations.
You’re experiencing the same thing now, because stress is a normal bodily response. You can manage it and even use it to your advantage.
Dial down media consumption. In these uncertain times, the world craves information. Knowledge tempers anxiety about the virus, and knowing what precautions to take makes us feel safer. But it’s easy to get overloaded in a 24-hour news cycle. First, make sure the information you’re consuming is reliable. The internet can be a muddle of semi-truthful muck. Second, limit the amount of mainstream news you consume daily. Mainstream news tends to lean on sensationalism, and depressing news we can’t control affects us.
Do something you’ve always wanted. As Atticus once said in a poem, “Life is like an hourglass. Each grain of sand is a moment that passes.” This may be just a locution, but it’s profound today. Everyone is at home and has so much free time. Yet we become anxious when we realize we’re wasting it. Productivity gets our minds off the virus. Now is a perfect time to start the first chapter of that book you’ve been meaning to read or crystallize that business plan you’ve been contemplating. Do something that your future self will be proud of when all is said and done.
Help others. Giving is a powerful neural pathway to happiness. Our brains are hardwired to release oxytocin, serotonin and dopamine, the trifecta of happiness, in response to altruism. While money helps, you can also give time, talents and expertise — there’s no shortage of people who would appreciate that now.
Take care of yourself. Mental well-being and physical health are the two sides of the same coin — the body and mind. Monitor your physical condition. The pandemic has left our routines in shambles. We exercise less, binge-watch Netflix and eat embarrassing amounts of junk food. This is the ugly side of staying home. We refuse to let the virus hijack parts of our lives that we can control. This new normal is hard but shouldn’t be hopeless.
